title: A. Equal Subsequences
statement:
We call a bitstring^{∗} perfect if it has the same number of mathtt101 and mathtt010 subsequences^{†}. Construct a perfect bitstring of length n where the number of mathtt1 characters it contains is exactly k.

It can be proven that the construction is always possible. If there are multiple solutions, output any of them.

^{∗}A bitstring is a string consisting only of the characters mathtt0 and mathtt1.

^{†}A sequence a is a subsequence of a string b if a can be obtained from b by the deletion of several (possibly zero or all) characters.

Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases t (1 ≤ t ≤ 500). The description of the test cases follows.

The first line of each test case contains two integers n and k (1 ≤ n ≤ 100, 0 ≤ k ≤ n) — the size of the bitstring and the number of mathtt1 characters in the bitstring.

For each test case, output the constructed bitstring. If there are multiple solutions, output any of them.

In the first test case, the number of mathtt101 and mathtt010 subsequences is the same, both being 1, and the sequence contains exactly two mathtt1 characters.

In the second test case, the number of mathtt101 and mathtt010 subsequences is the same, both being 2, and the sequence contains exactly three mathtt1 characters.

In the third test case, the number of mathtt101 and mathtt010 subsequences is the same, both being 0, and the sequence contains exactly five mathtt1 characters.

Input:
```
54 25 35 56 21 1
```

Output:
```
1010
10110
11111
100010
1
```
